title: Present Simple Negatives (Don't / Doesn't)
description: Form negative statements in the present simple using do not (don't) and does not (doesn't).
objectives: Use 'do not / don't' with I, you, we, and they + base verb
Use 'does not / doesn't' with he, she, and it + base verb (never adding -s to the main verb!)
Correct the common error of double-marking ('He doesn't works' -> 'He doesn't work')

sections.title: Forming Negatives with Auxiliary 'Do' & 'Does'
sections.content:
To make a present simple statement negative, English uses the **auxiliary verb (helping verb)** **do / does** combined with **not**.

### The Golden Rule of Negatives
When **does** or **doesn't** appears in a sentence, it carries the third-person marker. Therefore, the main verb **REVERTS TO ITS BARE BASE FORM (V1)**!
- Affirmative: *He works.*
- Negative: *He **does not work**.* (NEVER *'He doesn't works'*!).

tables.title: Form / Use / Signal Words / Common Mistakes
rows: I don't know / He doesn't go
Full form 'do not' used for formal writing.

callouts.title: The S-Theft Rule
callouts.text: Think of **doesn't** as a thief that steals the '-s' from the main verb! Once **doesn't** takes the -s, the main verb must remain bare: **He doesn't eat** (not eats).

callouts.title: Never Use 'No' Before a Verb
callouts.text: Urdu speakers sometimes say *'I no like'* or *'He no work'*. In English, you MUST use **don't** or **doesn't** before action verbs.

timeline.title: Absence of Habit Across Time
timeline.present: He does not smoke (Ongoing non-action / habit)
timeline.explanation: Present simple negative describes an ongoing refusal, habit absence, or state of untruth.

sections.title: Lesson Summary
sections.content: What you learned about Present Simple negatives:
summaryPoints: Use don't (do not) with I, you, we, they + base verb.
Use doesn't (does not) with he, she, it + base verb.
NEVER keep the -s on the main verb after doesn't (He doesn't work, NOT doesn't works).
Never say 'I no like' or 'He no work' in English.
Contractions (don't, doesn't) are standard in natural speaking.
